passage: You asked how I got calmer in quizzes, Naveen? My speech used to race. In the quiz round I'd say the whole answer in one breath, like a train with no brakes, and then blank at the end. I'm Farhan, and my nerves were so loud I couldn't hear myself. You told me, "You sound like a train." I laughed, but it helped. So I practised: breathe out first, then speak, then stop at every full stop. Just stop. It felt slow, almost silly. But halfway through the next quiz my hands weren't shaking. The steadier pace made me feel calmer, not just sound it.

qa.q: What did Naveen say Farhan sounded like?
qa.a: Naveen said Farhan sounded like a train.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when the speech raced in quizzes?
qa.a: Farhan was nervous, and the nerves were so loud that Farhan couldn't hear the words. Racing speech was part of that anxiety.

qa.q: What could Farhan do before answering a quiz question?
qa.a: Breathe out first, then speak, and stop at every full stop. A steadier pace helps Farhan feel calmer as well as sound calmer.

qa.q: How might Naveen's train comment have felt to Farhan?
qa.a: Farhan laughed, so it landed lightly, and it helped Farhan see how the speech sounded. It was said as a friend.

grounding: A teenager whose speech races when anxious practises a measured pace, and it helps the teenager feel calmer.

passage: Sonali had to read the morning announcements, and I stood at the side of the hall. She started so fast that the words ran together. Her hands gripped the paper. Then she stopped at a full stop, breathed out audibly and started again more slowly. Her shoulders came down a little. By the third sentence the whole hall could hear her. I can't know what she felt inside. Maybe she was nervous, maybe just wanting to finish. But her pace changed, and afterwards she said, "That was better when I stopped." I'm Mehak, and I told her it sounded steady.

qa.q: Where did Mehak stand while Sonali read announcements?
qa.a: Mehak stood at the side of the hall.

qa.q: What was Sonali probably feeling when she began so fast, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was probably nervous, since her hands gripped the paper and the words ran together. Mehak admits not knowing for sure.

qa.q: What could Sonali do again before her next announcement?
qa.a: Stop at each full stop and breathe out before starting. The slower pace helps her sound and feel calmer.

qa.q: How might the hall have heard Sonali's change of pace?
qa.a: They could hear her clearly by the third sentence, which likely made her sound more confident. It may also have helped her relax.

grounding: A teenager whose speech races when anxious pauses at full stops and breathes out, and a classmate observes the steadier pace.

passage:
Monday: At debate practice, Kamal raced through his speech so fast the words blurred together. He finished in half the time and was out of breath. Parul Ma'am said, "I didn't catch your second point. Your heart's running and dragging your mouth with it."
Wednesday: Ma'am showed him a trick. Breathe out before starting. Pause at every full stop, count one in your head. Kamal practised in the empty classroom, feeling silly at first.
Friday: At the inter-house debate, his hands still shook. But he breathed out, started slowly, and paused at each full stop. By the second point, his heart had slowed too. He actually noticed the audience nodding.
Afterwards he told Ma'am, "It's weird. When I talked slower, I felt less scared."

qa.q: What did Parul Ma'am say Kamal's heart was doing?
qa.a: Running and dragging his mouth with it.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when he raced through his speech on Monday?
qa.a: Kamal felt anxious and nervous, which made his speech rush out of control.

qa.q: What small steps helped Kamal slow down?
qa.a: Breathing out before starting and pausing for a count at each full stop.

qa.q: How might the audience have experienced the change between Monday and Friday?
qa.a: On Monday they could hardly follow him, but on Friday they could understand his points and nodded along.

grounding: Over a week, a teenager whose speech races with anxiety practises pausing and breathing, and feels calmer as well as sounding calmer.

passage:
"Harsha, you think you talk fast when you're nervous? Let your Urmila Mausi tell you something.
When I was sixteen, I was chosen to read the news on All-School Radio. I was so scared that I read the whole page in two minutes. My teacher told me afterward that nobody understood a word.
I cried in the washroom. Then she came and found me. She said, 'Breathe out before you start. Then pause at every full stop, like you're stepping on stones in a river.'
Next week I tried it. Pause, breathe, next sentence. I didn't just sound calmer. I actually felt calmer, and I could hear my own voice for the first time.
So tomorrow, before your presentation, remember: stepping stones."

qa.q: What was Urmila chosen to read?
qa.a: The news on All-School Radio.

qa.q: What was young Urmila feeling when she cried in the washroom?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and disappointed after rushing the news because of nerves.

qa.q: What choice inside the story helped Urmila?
qa.a: Her teacher chose to come find her and teach her to breathe out and pause at full stops, which helped her feel and sound calmer.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt when Urmila read calmly the next week?
qa.a: The teacher probably felt proud and pleased that the advice worked.

grounding: An aunt recalls rushing her speech from nerves and learning to breathe out and pause, which made her feel calmer.

passage:
The prefect interview was supposed to be at three, but the power had gone, the room was stuffy, and Lakshmi had run all the way from the bus stop. She sat down, sweaty and breathless, and started talking before anyone asked.
"I-want-to-be-prefect-because-I-care-about-the-school-and-I-organised-the-food-drive-and-"
Jeevan, the head prefect on the panel, held up a hand gently. "Take a breath. We've got time."
Lakshmi stopped. She breathed out slowly. Then she started again, pausing at each full stop, like she'd practised at home.
"I want to be prefect because I care about this school. Last year, I organised the food drive."
By the end, her shoulders had dropped, and her voice had steadied. The panel smiled.

qa.q: What had Lakshmi organised last year?
qa.a: The food drive.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when she started talking so fast?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt anxious and flustered after running, with the hot room adding to her nerves.

qa.q: What helped Lakshmi slow down?
qa.a: Jeevan's calm invitation to breathe, and her practised habit of breathing out and pausing at full stops.

qa.q: How might the panel have seen Lakshmi's first rushed words?
qa.a: They probably saw she was nervous and flustered, not unprepared, which is why Jeevan gently slowed her down.

grounding: Under pressure, a teenager's rushed speech steadies when she breathes out and pauses at full stops, and she feels calmer.

passage: Elizabeth's first run-through of the model-UN speech lasted fifty seconds. It was meant to take two minutes. Payal, sitting cross-legged on the bed in their Bandra flat with a phone timer, blinked. "You swallowed half the words. I heard 'climate' and then just wind." Elizabeth laughed, but her hands were cold and her heart was thumping the way it always did before a stage. "When I'm nervous my mouth just runs." "Then give it speed bumps," Payal said. She took a pencil and circled every full stop on the printout. "At each circle, stop. Let the air out, then in, then the next line." The second run was clumsy; Elizabeth kept forgetting the circles. The third time she let each breath out slowly, and the speech stretched to one minute fifty. "Better?" Payal asked. Elizabeth nodded, surprised. "It wasn't only slower. My hands stopped shaking."

qa.q: How long did Elizabeth's first run-through last?
qa.a: It lasted fifty seconds, though it was meant to take two minutes.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth's racing speech suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She was most likely anxious: her hands were cold and her heart was thumping, as before a stage. Part of it may also have been wanting to get the speech over with.

qa.q: What small step helped Elizabeth slow down?
qa.a: Payal circled every full stop so Elizabeth would stop there and let the air out before the next line, and practising it three times made it stick.

qa.q: What was it like for Payal to listen to the first run?
qa.a: Payal could hardly follow it, catching only 'climate' and then wind, so Payal wanted to help Elizabeth be heard, not just finish.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose speech races with nerves practising pauses at full stops with a breath out, and finding that a steadier pace also calms her body.
